c.tagline: Spice isle capital where a horseshoe harbor meets Caribbean beaches.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are unmetered; fares are fixed by zone and set by taxi associations (e.g. Grenada Airport Taxi Association) - agree the rate before departure.

emergency.note: 911 is the national emergency number for police, fire and ambulance; General Hospital in St. George's is the main referral hospital.

avoid.reason: Watch belongings on Grand Anse beach and in market areas, and avoid poorly lit streets late at night.

hood_desc: Grenada's most famous two-mile white-sand beach lined with resorts, dive shops and beach bars; the easiest, most walkable base for first-time visitors.
A lively hillside enclave around a working fishing bay and marina next to St. George's University, popular with SGU students, sailors and families who want a residential feel with restaurants nearby.
A quiet, upscale peninsula of villas and cottages around Prickly Bay favored by yachties and long-stay visitors wanting calm water and a residential, low-key vibe close to the airport.
A smaller, mellower beach bay just south of Grand Anse dotted with boutique and villa resorts, best suited to couples and honeymooners seeking upscale seclusion.
The historic horseshoe harbor and commercial heart of the capital, with forts, markets and colonial buildings, ideal for culture-focused travelers who don't need to be beachfront.

water.note: Officially treated and safe, but many locals and hotels still recommend bottled water for visitors.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (Eastern Caribbean dollars) directly to the driver or conductor when boarding or alighting; there are no fare cards, passes or apps. Exact or small change is appreciated.
transit.hours: Minibuses generally run about 6:00am-9:00pm Monday-Saturday with sharply reduced or no service on Sundays and public holidays; there is no formal night bus service.
transit.note: Grenada has no rail or metro system; privately owned minibuses cover fixed routes island-wide from the Esplanade/Market Square terminal in St. George's, supplemented by taxis and the Osprey inter-island ferry.

tip.r: A 10% service charge is often already added to restaurant bills; if not included, a 10% tip is appreciated. Taxi drivers and hotel porters are tipped modestly at traveler's discretion.

food.name: Oil down
food.desc: Grenada's national dish: breadfruit, salted meat, dumplings and callaloo simmered down in turmeric-yellow coconut milk until the pot goes dry.

places.name: Patrick's Local Homestyle Restaurant
places.note: Long-running homestyle kitchen known for parades of small Grenadian dishes including oil down.

places.name: Dodgy Dock
places.note: Waterside restaurant with a regular local-food night; a good introduction to oil down.

places.name: Deyna's Tasty Food
places.note: Busy downtown canteen where Grenadians eat lunch; ask what is in the pot that day.

food.name: Callaloo soup
food.desc: Dasheen leaves blended with coconut milk, okra and spices into a smooth green soup, sometimes with crab or salt pork.

places.name: BB's Crabback Caribbean Restaurant
places.note: Harbourfront Grenadian kitchen known for callaloo and crab dishes.

places.name: Deyna's Tasty Food
places.note: Cheap, generous local soups and provisions in the middle of town.

places.name: Patrick's Local Homestyle Restaurant
places.note: Serves callaloo as part of its multi-dish Grenadian tasting spread.

food.name: Crab back & lambi (conch)
food.desc: Land-crab meat seasoned and baked back in the shell, and conch stewed or curried until tender - the island's two great shellfish plates.

places.name: BB's Crabback Caribbean Restaurant
places.note: Named for the dish; the obvious place to try crab back with a harbour view.

places.name: Coconut Beach Restaurant
places.note: Long-established French-Creole beach restaurant with seafood cooked to order in the sand.

places.name: The Aquarium Restaurant
places.note: Beachside spot known for seafood and its Sunday barbecue.

food.name: Grilled fresh fish
food.desc: Tuna, mahi-mahi, snapper and wahoo landed that morning, rubbed with green seasoning and grilled with rice, provisions and plantain.

places.name: Gouyave Fish Friday
places.note: Weekly street fish festival; the island's best-known food night, worth the drive.

places.name: Umbrellas Beach Bar
places.note: Casual two-storey beach bar doing grilled catch and cold drinks all day.

places.name: Coconut Beach Restaurant
places.note: Fish grilled Creole-style with garlic and lime, right on the sand.

food.name: Roti
food.desc: Soft flatbread wrapped around curried chicken, goat, conch or vegetables with potato and chickpeas - the standard Grenadian lunch on the go.

places.name: The Nutmeg
places.note: Institution on the upper floor above the harbour, known for roti, rum punch and the view.

places.name: Deyna's Tasty Food
places.note: Reliable, filling rotis and local plates at local prices.

places.name: St. George's Market Square
places.note: Vendors sell roti and snacks around the market, best on Saturday mornings.

food.name: Nutmeg ice cream
food.desc: Grenada grows a fifth of the world's nutmeg and puts it in ice cream - warm, spicy and unlike anything else in the Caribbean.

places.name: House of Chocolate
places.note: Small cocoa museum and cafe doing nutmeg and chocolate ice cream, plus cocoa tea.

places.name: The Nutmeg
places.note: Old-school harbour restaurant with nutmeg desserts on the menu.

places.name: IGA Supermarket
places.note: Locally made nutmeg ice cream by the tub if you want it to take away.

food.name: Rum punch & Grenadian rum
food.desc: One of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak - always grated with nutmeg on top. Local rums include Clarke's Court and River Antoine.

places.name: The Nutmeg
places.note: Famous for its rum punch overlooking the harbour; a Grenada rite of passage.

places.name: Umbrellas Beach Bar
places.note: Sunset rum punch on the beach, popular with locals and visitors alike.

places.name: Clarke's Court Rum Distillery
places.note: Working distillery south of town with tours and tastings of the island's best-known rum.

food.name: Cocoa tea & local juices
food.desc: Grated Grenadian cocoa boiled with cinnamon, nutmeg and milk, plus soursop, sorrel and mauby juices sold cold at the market.

places.name: House of Chocolate
places.note: Cocoa tea made from Grenadian beans, with an exhibit on the island's chocolate.

places.name: St. George's Market Square
places.note: Spice and juice vendors sell sorrel, soursop and mauby, busiest Saturday morning.

places.name: Deyna's Tasty Food
places.note: Fresh local juices by the glass with lunch, including seasonal fruit.

landmarks: The Carenage
The picturesque horseshoe-shaped inner harbor lined with pastel colonial buildings, fishing boats, and waterfront restaurants — the postcard image of Saint George's.
Fort George
Grenada's oldest fort, perched on a headland above the harbor entrance, offering cannons, tunnels, and sweeping views over the capital and Caribbean Sea.
Grand Anse Beach
A two-mile crescent of soft white sand and calm turquoise water just outside town, consistently ranked among the Caribbean's most beautiful beaches.
St. George's Anglican Church (ruins)
The atmospheric roofless ruins of a historic 1825 church, damaged by Hurricane Ivan, now standing as a hauntingly beautiful memorial and photo spot.
Market Square
A colorful, aromatic hub where vendors sell nutmeg, spices, and produce — a vivid reminder that Grenada is the 'Isle of Spice.'
York House and Parliament Building
Elegant Georgian-era government buildings that showcase the island's colonial architectural heritage in the heart of the capital.
Grenada National Museum
Housed in an 18th-century former French army barracks and prison, this museum traces the island's Amerindian, colonial, and independence history.
Fort Frederick
Built by the French and completed by the British, this hilltop fort offers some of the best panoramic views of Saint George's and its harbor.
Sendall Tunnel
A quirky 19th-century tunnel carved through a hill, connecting the Carenage to the Esplanade and standing as a distinctive engineering landmark of the old town.
Bay Gardens Botanical Reserve
A lush hillside garden overlooking the city, home to native and tropical plant species and a peaceful escape from the bustle of the harbor below.

train.note: Grenada has no railway. Get around by minibus, taxi or the domestic ferry.

bus.note: No international buses (island). Privately run route minibuses cover Grenada from the Melville Street Bus Terminal in St. George's.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferry from Grenada; regional islands are reached by air. The Osprey fast ferry (https://www.ospreylines.com/) is domestic only, running from The Carenage in St. George's to Carriacou and Petite Martinique.
